name: DZY Loves Colors
description: DZY loves colors, and he enjoys painting. On a colorful day, DZY gets a colorful ribbon, which consists of n units (they are numbered from 1 to n from left to right). The color of the i -th unit of the ribbon is i at first. It is colorful enough, but we still consider that the colorfulness of each unit is 0 at first. DZY loves painting, we know. He takes up a paintbrush with color x and uses it to draw a line on the ribbon. In such a case some contiguous units are painted. Imagine that the color of unit i currently is y . When it is painted by this paintbrush, the color of the unit becomes x , and the colorfulness of the unit increases by | x - y | . DZY wants to perform m operations, each operation can be one of the following: Paint all the units with numbers between l and r (both inclusive) with color x . Ask the sum of colorfulness of the units between l and r (both inclusive). Can you help DZY?
input_specification: The first line contains two space-separated integers n , m (1 ≤ n , m ≤ 10 5 ) . Each of the next m lines begins with a integer type (1 ≤ type ≤ 2) , which represents the type of this operation. If type = 1 , there will be 3 more integers l , r , x (1 ≤ l ≤ r ≤ n ; 1 ≤ x ≤ 10 8 ) in this line, describing an operation 1 . If type = 2 , there will be 2 more integers l , r (1 ≤ l ≤ r ≤ n ) in this line, describing an operation 2 .
output_specification: For each operation 2 , print a line containing the answer — sum of colorfulness.
approach_summary: Build a Segment Tree over the array. Implement point update and associative range query operations in O(log N) time per query.

topic_editorial.title: Editorial: 444C — DZY Loves Colors [57. Segment Tree (Point Update Range Query)]
topic_editorial.summary: Range queries and updates via Segment Tree.
topic_editorial.key_invariant: The query operation is associative (e.g., sum, min, max, gcd). Any contiguous range $[L, R]$ can be decomposed into at most $O(\log N)$ canonical dyadic intervals represented by nodes in a binary tree.
topic_editorial.solution_walkthrough:
### Step 1: Tree Construction
We build a binary segment tree over array $A[1..N]$.
Each node covers a segment $[L, R]$. If $L = R$, the node stores $A[L]$. Otherwise:
$$\text{node.val} = \text{combine}(\text{left\_child.val}, \text{right\_child.val})$$

### Step 2: Point / Range Updates
To update position $pos$ with value $val$:
- Traverse down to the leaf node $[pos, pos]$.
- Update leaf value.
- Recompute ancestor values on the way back up in $O(\log N)$ time.

### Step 3: Range Query Processing
To query the associative aggregate on range $[qL, qR]$:
- If current segment $[L, R]$ is completely within $[qL, qR]$, return node value.
- If disjoint, return identity element.
- Otherwise, split and return $\text{combine}(\text{query}(left), \text{query}(right))$.
topic_editorial.complexity_analysis:
- **Time Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}((N + Q) \log N)$
  Building the segment tree takes $\mathcal{O}(N)$. Each point/range query and update traverses at most $4 \log N$ tree nodes, requiring $\mathcal{O}(\log N)$ time per query.
- **Space Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(N)$
  A standard binary segment tree requires at most $4N$ nodes to represent elements up to index $N$.
